title: The switch Statement
objectives: Write switch statements with correct syntax.
Identify when switch is better than if...else.
theory: A switch statement is useful when a single variable has many possible values. Instead of a long chain of else if statements, switch provides a cleaner syntax.
The syntax is switch (expression) { case value1: code; break; case value2: code; break; default: code; }. The expression is evaluated once. Each case compares to the expression value.
The break keyword exits the switch. Without break, execution continues to the next case, causing unintended behavior. Most cases need break unless intentionally falling through.
The default case handles unexpected values. It is like the final else in an if...else chain. Default is optional but recommended for safety.

Switch works well for menu selection, day of the week, game states, or any situation with discrete, predictable values. Switch is clearer than else if when comparing one variable to multiple constants.
terms: Tests one expression against multiple values.
A label matching a specific value.
tryIt: Create a switch that translates a number 1-3 into a colour name.
challenge: Build a calculator menu using switch to select between +, −, *, and / operations.
mistakes: Each case needs a value, not a condition.
summary: Switch tests one expression against multiple values. Each case needs break. Default handles unexpected cases. Use switch when comparing one variable to many constants.
quiz: When is switch better than if...else?
For one variable with many possible values
Switch is cleaner for discrete values.
Break prevents fall-through to the next case.
Missing break causes execution to continue to the next case.
Result of switch (3) with no matching case and no default?
Without default, unmatched cases do nothing.
